title: An 8,000 km quantum-safe network, with quantum keys on the short links only
summary: Seven research networks, universities and companies linked Chicago, Amsterdam and the Bilbao area at SC26 with a network secured by two technologies at once. Quantum key distribution protected two links of 25 km and under; the transatlantic and European spans used post-quantum cryptography, with keys relayed through intermediate sites.

banner.alt: Illustration: two pairs of nearby network nodes joined by short wavy links, connected through a middle node by long dashed arcs, with small squares on either side of the middle node.

key_points: On 18 November 2026, at the SC26 conference in Chicago, the University of the Basque Country (EHU), Luxquanta, Ciena, GÉANT, PCSS, RedIRIS and SURF announced a demonstration network linking Chicago, Amsterdam and Bilbao, about 8,000 km in all.
Quantum key distribution ran only on two short fibre links: under 1 km between two booths in Chicago, and 25 km between two university sites in Bizkaia, Spain.

The long spans, about 1,200 km from the Bilbao area to Amsterdam and about 7,000 km from Amsterdam to Chicago, used post-quantum cryptography with the NIST standard ML-KEM; no quantum signal crossed the Atlantic.
The new element is orchestration: one framework, EHU's QuLore, chose a key source for each connection and made three key-management systems work together.
The release gives no key rates, error figures or independent assessment, and it does not say whether the sites that relay keys can read them.
author: Quantum Research Center

sections.heading: What was announced
paragraphs: On 18 November 2026 a group of seven organizations announced a demonstration of what they call hybrid quantum-safe networking, shown at SC26, the supercomputing conference in Chicago. The release, published by the quantum-cryptography company Luxquanta on behalf of the partners, names the University of the Basque Country (EHU), Luxquanta, the optical-networking company Ciena, the European research network GÉANT, the Polish computing centre PCSS, the Spanish research network RedIRIS and the Dutch research network SURF. The Quantum Insider carried the release the same day, and Quantum Computing Report summarized it on 20 November.

The network had five nodes in three places. Two sat at the Ciena and PCSS booths at SC26, less than 1 km apart. One was at SURF in Amsterdam. Two were at EHU sites in Bilbao and Zamudio, in the Spanish province of Bizkaia, 25 km apart. The partners describe the whole as spanning about 8,000 km and protecting optical links, network tunnels and a live video call. It is a demonstration network, not a deployed service, and the release gives no date for any production use.

sections.heading: Where quantum keys were used, and where they were not
paragraphs: Two technologies protect against a future quantum computer breaking today's public-key encryption. Quantum key distribution, QKD, sends light in quantum states through fibre so that two ends share a key whose secrecy rests on physics; the signal fades in fibre, and the release itself puts its useful range at roughly 100 km. Post-quantum cryptography, PQC, is ordinary software based on mathematical problems believed to resist quantum computers, and it works at any distance over the existing internet. The background is in our explainer on quantum-safe security.

The demonstration used each where it fits. Luxquanta's continuous-variable QKD systems, which encode keys in the amplitude and phase of weak laser light, ran on the two short links. Ciena's equipment carried the quantum signal, the QKD systems' own coordination channel and the encrypted data on a single fibre pair, and its line-rate encryptors, at 1.6 terabits per second in Chicago and 800 gigabits per second in Bizkaia, mixed the QKD keys with keys from post-quantum algorithms. The two long spans used PQC alone, with keys agreed through ML-KEM, the key-establishment standard NIST published in August 2024 as FIPS 203. The 8,000 km figure therefore describes the network, not the reach of any quantum link.

sections.heading: What the software layer did
paragraphs: The part the partners present as new is the coordination. EHU's i2T group built QuLore, a framework that acts as a security orchestrator. When an application asks for a key, QuLore checks what the two endpoints and the network between them can offer, picks the strongest quantum-safe option and coordinates the systems that manage keys. Three such systems took part, from Luxquanta, from EHU and SURF's open-source eduKMS in Amsterdam, and the release says they worked together through standard interfaces, without naming which standard.

Data were protected at three levels. Ciena's equipment encrypted the light in the fibre on the short links; IPsec tunnels, the usual way to encrypt traffic between sites, protected the long links; and a modified open-source video-call program encrypted audio and video end to end, with a separate key for each direction of each stream. Where two endpoints had no direct QKD link, as between Chicago and Bilbao, the key was relayed through intermediate sites, including SURF's node in Amsterdam, so that both ends ended up holding the same key. The partners say the post-quantum links stand in for future QKD links, for example via satellite, once those exist.

sections.heading: What the demonstration does not show
paragraphs: The release gives no key rates, no error rates and no figures for how much traffic each key protected, and we found no paper or independent evaluation. It shows that equipment and software from several vendors and research groups can be made to work together across a mixed network, which is an engineering result. It does not show long-distance quantum communication, and it does not compare the security of the combined system with PQC alone.

Key relaying deserves a closer look. In a relay, an intermediate site normally receives the key in usable form before passing it on, which is why such sites are called trusted nodes; the release does not say how QuLore handles this, so whether the Amsterdam node could read the transatlantic keys is not stated. Security agencies are cautious about QKD for related reasons. The UK National Cyber Security Centre, in guidance updated in August 2025, points out that QKD does not authenticate the parties and must be paired with other cryptography, recommends PQC as the primary defence, will not support QKD for government or military use, and advises other sectors not to rely on QKD alone. The demonstration's design, PQC everywhere and QKD added on two short links, is consistent with that advice; whether the QKD layer adds enough protection to justify its hardware is the question the partners have not yet answered with data.
